summary: For children aged 6-7, teach how the shapes of solid objects can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching, with the key insight that materials respond DIFFERENTLY: some spring back (elastic), some keep the new shape (plastic/permanent), and some barely change this way (rigid). Keep the enquiry on the MATERIAL an object is made from, and make explicit that changing the shape does not change what the material is and makes no new material. The central misconception to confront is over-generalised elasticity (expecting everything to spring back). The strongest activity lets children apply a force first-hand and then release to witness the spring-back-vs-stay contrast; a hands-on tray of real dough, elastic and sponge is the natural companion, with a screen or picture version as a scaffold that offers a different experience.
misconceptions: Over-generalised elasticity — assuming ALL objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will spring back to their original shape (the central Y2 misconception).
Believing a physical shape change cannot be undone at all — or conversely that it always can.
Thinking that changing an object's shape changes the material it is made of (it does not — no new material forms).
Testing the OBJECT rather than the material, so results are attributed to the item ('the spoon') not the substance ('metal').
Assuming a rigid material (wood, stone) simply hasn't been pushed hard enough, rather than that some materials do not change shape this way.

activities.title: Materials deformation bench: apply a force, then let go
steps: Choose a material from a varied set — playdough/plasticine, an elastic band, a sponge, a thick wooden stick or block, a stone, soft wire, paper.
Pick one of the four actions and apply it: press/squeeze to squash, curve it to bend, hold each end and turn opposite ways to twist, pull to stretch.
Watch the material deform as the force is applied (dough flattens, wire coils, elastic thins).
Release ('let go') and observe what happens: does it snap back to its old shape, stay in the new shape, or barely move?
Record the result for each material and the action you used in a comparison grid: springs back / stays changed / won't change this way.
Note each time that the material is still the same stuff — e.g. a tag or label 'this is still WOOD' — so the shape changed but the material did not.
activities.insight: Materials respond differently to the same action: squeeze a sponge and it springs back, squeeze dough and it stays flattened, and squeeze a thick wooden stick or a stone and it barely changes. Likewise, a stretched elastic band snaps back while twisted soft wire stays twisted. So 'everything springs back' is not true, and the result can depend on the action as well as the material. Across all of this, the material itself is unchanged.

activities.title: Embody and define the four actions
steps: Learn each action with a precise, embodied definition: squash = press/squeeze; bend = curve so it is not straight; twist = hold each end and turn opposite ways; stretch = pull to change its shape.
Perform each action with your own hands first (turn your hands to twist, pull to stretch) before touching a material.
Match each action word to a demonstration or picture of that action.
Say the definition aloud (with audio support for pre/early readers).
activities.insight: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching are four distinct actions, not one generic 'push'. Being able to produce each one distinctly is needed before comparing how materials respond.

activities.title: Predict, then test, and sort by how materials respond
steps: Before handling each material, predict how it will respond to a chosen action: will it spring back, stay changed, or barely change?
Test your prediction by hand and compare what happened to what you expected.

Sort the materials into three groups for the action you tested (a different action can give a different result): springs back (e.g. squeezed sponge, stretched elastic band), stays changed (e.g. squashed dough, bent soft wire), won't change this way by hand (e.g. squeezed thick wood, stone).
Build a simple table with the material down the side and columns for 'springs back?', 'stays changed?', 'won't change?'.
activities.insight: Predicting first surfaces your idea so the evidence can confirm or overturn it; recording in a table supports comparing and classifying materials by how they respond.

activities.title: Same material, new shape: show the stuff is unchanged
steps: Take a lump of clay, roll it into a ball, then squash it flat — look at the before and after.
Explain whether it is still clay after being squashed, and how you could show it is the same stuff (e.g. roll it back into a ball).
Weigh a ball of clay, squash it, and weigh it again; compare the two weights.
Do the same reasoning for a bent metal paperclip: is it still metal after bending?
activities.insight: Changing an object's shape does not change the material it is made of and does not make new material — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal, and the weight stays the same because nothing was added or taken away.

checkQuestion: Put out a lump of clay, a sponge, an elastic band, a wooden lolly stick and a metal paperclip. Say: 'Try to change each one's shape by squashing, bending, twisting or stretching. Which keep their new shape and which spring back? And for each — after you've changed it, is it still the SAME material?' Watch them work.
checkAnswer: Produces the four distinct actions; observes that some materials hold the new shape (clay squashed, paperclip bent) while others spring back (elastic band, sponge), and that some barely change (wood); states the material itself is unchanged — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal.
